---
title: "How To Use Login Hooks And Custom Claims"
description: "Allow or deny sign-ins with a post_login hook, add claims with a pre_token hook, set static custom claims per role and OpenID client, and port Auth0 Actions and Rules to them."
sidebar:
  order: 11.7
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'

Use this guide when a sign-in has to ask your own system something before it completes, such as
"is this account suspended in billing", or when tokens need values your backend reads, such as a
plan or a tenant id. It is also the guide for porting Auth0 Actions and Rules.

There are two tools, and most apps need only the second:

- **Static custom claims**: a fixed JSON object attached to an instance role, an organization role
  or an OpenID Provider client. Everyone holding the role gets the claims. No code runs.
- **Login hooks**: an HTTPS endpoint you run that the auth API calls during sign-in. `post_login`
  allows or denies. `pre_token` allows, denies, or adds claims computed per user.

Hook calls are signed the same way as [webhooks](/build/webhooks), so your hook service can prove a
call came from your Seamless Auth instance.

<Aside type="note" title="Needs auth API v0.23.0">
Login hooks, custom claims and every route on this page need `seamless-auth-api` v0.23.0 or later.
Custom claims in OpenID Provider tokens also need the provider at 0.4.0 (see
[Versions](#versions)).
</Aside>

---

## Where Each Runs

| Moment                                            | `post_login` | `pre_token` | Static claims |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ----------- | ------------- |
| Sign-in, once the factor is proven, before the session exists | Called | Called right after `post_login` | Resolved |
| Organization switch (`POST /organizations/:id/switch`) | Not called | Called, with the new organization | Resolved |
| Token refresh                                     | Not called   | **Not called**. The claims it gave are kept on the session | **Resolved again** |
| Session exchange (a child session)                | Not called   | Not called. The child copies the parent's hook claims | Resolved |
| Break-glass administrator sign-in                 | **Never**    | **Never**   | Resolved |
| Recovery session (account recovery, recovery code) | **Never**   | **Never**   | None. A recovery token carries no custom claims |

Two consequences to plan around:

- **`pre_token` claims are as fresh as the session, not the token.** A value your hook returned at
  sign-in stays in every token of that session until the user signs in again or switches
  organization. If the value can change during a session (a plan upgrade, a suspension), either
  read it live in your backend or accept that it applies at the next sign-in.
- **Static claims follow the user's roles at each token.** They are resolved on every mint,
  including refresh, so a changed set or role reaches the user within `access_token_ttl`.

Break-glass and recovery never call a hook so that a hook which is down cannot lock out the
administrator who would fix it, or a user enrolling a new factor.

---

## Login Hooks

One hook per trigger (`post_login`, `pre_token`), each with its own URL, timeout, failure mode and
signing secret.

### The Call

The auth API sends a `POST` with the three signature headers (`webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`,
`webhook-signature`) and this body, `LoginHookCallSchema` in `@seamless-auth/types` 0.39.0:

```json
{
  "id": "3f2e1d0c-9b8a-4765-8432-10fedcba9876",
  "trigger": "pre_token",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-07T12:00:00.000Z",
  "user": {
    "id": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
    "email": "ana@example.com",
    "phone": null,
    "roles": ["user"]
  },
  "method": "passkey",
  "organization": { "id": "44444444-4444-4444-8444-444444444444", "roles": ["admin"] },
  "client": null,
  "request": { "ipAddress": "203.0.113.9", "userAgent": "Mozilla/5.0 ..." }
}
```

| Field          | Meaning |
| -------------- | ------- |
| `id`           | The invocation id, equal to `webhook-id` |
| `trigger`      | `post_login` or `pre_token` |
| `user`         | The user and their instance roles |
| `method`       | How the sign-in completed, such as `passkey`, `email_otp`, `phone_otp`, `totp`, `magic_link` or `oauth`. `null` on an organization switch |
| `organization` | The organization the session is in and the member's roles there, or `null` |
| `client`       | Always `null` for now. No first-party sign-in knows which OpenID Provider client it is for (seamless-auth-oidc-provider#47) |
| `request`      | The caller's IP address and user agent |

The body is parsed through the schema before it is sent, so it never carries a token, code,
cookie or secret.

### The Answer

Answer `200` with JSON. `post_login` (`PostLoginHookResultSchema`):

```json
{ "decision": "allow" }
```

```json
{
  "decision": "deny",
  "reason": "account is suspended in billing (ticket 4411)",
  "userMessage": "Your account is suspended. Contact your administrator."
}
```

`pre_token` (`PreTokenHookResultSchema`) takes the same fields plus `claims`:

```json
{ "decision": "allow", "claims": { "plan": "enterprise", "tenant": "44444444-4444-4444-8444-444444444444" } }
```

| Field         | Rules |
| ------------- | ----- |
| `decision`    | `allow` or `deny`. Required |
| `reason`      | Up to 500 characters. Written to the audit log (`login_hook_denied`) and **never shown** to the user, so it can hold internal detail |
| `userMessage` | Up to 200 characters of plain text. **Shown** to the user as the refusal's `message` |
| `claims`      | `pre_token` only. An object of custom claims, held to the [claim rules](#claim-names-and-reserved-claims). A `post_login` answer with `claims` has failed |

A deny's `claims` are ignored. Reserved claim names in an allow are stripped and the stripping is
audited (`login_hook_claims_stripped`). Any other claim that breaks the rules (a name outside the
pattern, nesting past depth 3, more than 1 KiB) fails the hook rather than being dropped.

### What The User Sees

The sign-in completion routes (`/webauthn/login/finish`, `/otp/verify-email-otp`,
`/otp/verify-login-email-otp`, `/otp/verify-login-phone-otp`, `/totp/verify-login`,
`/magic-link/check`, `/oauth/:providerId/callback`) and `POST /organizations/:id/switch` can answer:

| Situation                              | Status | Body |
| -------------------------------------- | ------ | ---- |
| A hook denied                          | 403    | `{"error":"login_denied","message":"<userMessage>"}`, with `message` only when the hook sent one |
| A hook with failure mode `closed` failed | 503  | `{"error":"login_hook_unavailable"}` |

No session is created on either, and the concurrent session limit has not run yet, so a refused
sign-in never costs the user a session they already had. Server adapters pass both bodies through
unchanged. In `@seamless-auth/react` and `@seamless-auth/client` the error's `message` is the
`error` code, and the hook's text is at `err.body.message`; the built-in views show fixed text, so
show `userMessage` yourself if you want it on screen.

### Timeouts And Failure Modes

- **Timeout:** 2000 ms by default, from 100 to 5000 ms. One attempt, never retried. The deadline
  covers the whole request, so a slow trickle of bytes cannot hold a sign-in open.
- **A failure** is a timeout, a connection that fails, a status outside 2xx (a redirect is never
  followed), a body that is not JSON or does not parse, a response over 64 KiB, or claims that
  break the rules.
- **`closed`** (the default): a failure refuses the sign-in with `503 login_hook_unavailable`.
- **`open`**: a failure is ignored, and the sign-in continues as if the hook did not exist, without
  its claims.

Every call is recorded with its outcome (`allowed`, `denied`, `failed_open`, `failed_closed`) in
the invocation log for 30 days, and audited as `login_hook_success`, `login_hook_denied` or
`login_hook_failed` (with the failure reason and status code).

| Pick     | When |
| -------- | ---- |
| `closed` | The hook enforces something: suspension, licensing, a compliance gate, an allow list. A sign-in your hook could not check should not complete. Also for a `pre_token` hook whose claims your backend authorizes with, unless your backend treats a missing claim as a denial |
| `open`   | The hook only adds convenience: claims your app can do without, or a soft check. Sign-in should keep working while your service is down |

With `open`, anything that makes your service slow or unreachable switches its denials off, so do
not use it for a deny that matters. With `closed`, your hook's availability is your sign-in's
availability for everyone except break-glass administrators and recovery. Keep it fast, run more
than one instance, and watch `failed_closed` in the invocation log.

### Set Up A Hook

Configure `CALLOUT_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (required in production once a hook exists) and, for a
hook service on a private address, `CALLOUT_PRIVATE_HOSTS`, as for webhooks
([Step 1 there](/build/webhooks#step-1-configure-the-auth-api)). The same URL rules apply: `https`
only in production, never the API's own host, and link-local addresses never.

**Console:** the **Login hooks** page (`/login-hooks` in `seamless-auth-admin-dashboard`) has one
section per trigger with the URL, timeout, failure mode, a test call, secret rotation and the
invocation log. It is in the console from v0.14.0.

**CLI:** `seamless-cli` 0.30.0 and later:

```bash
seamless hooks set post_login --url https://hooks.example.com/seamless   # prints the secret once
seamless hooks set pre_token --url https://hooks.example.com/seamless --failure-mode open
seamless hooks test post_login                                          # exits 1 when it fails
seamless hooks invocations post_login --outcome denied
seamless hooks set pre_token --disable                                  # changes only that setting
```

**Admin API:** reads need `admin:read`; writes, including the test call, need `admin:write` and a
fresh step-up ([How To Use TOTP And Step-Up](/build/totp-step-up)).

| Method   | Route                                        | Body or query                                   | Purpose |
| -------- | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `GET`    | `/admin/login-hooks`                         |                                                 | Both hooks (`{ hooks }`) |
| `PUT`    | `/admin/login-hooks/:trigger`                | `{ url, timeoutMs?, failureMode?, enabled? }`   | Create (`201`, with `secret` once) or replace (`200`, secret kept) |
| `GET`    | `/admin/login-hooks/:trigger`                |                                                 | One hook |
| `DELETE` | `/admin/login-hooks/:trigger`                |                                                 | Delete it. Sign-ins stop calling it |
| `POST`   | `/admin/login-hooks/:trigger/secret`         |                                                 | Rotate: `{ secret, previousSecretExpiresAt }` |
| `POST`   | `/admin/login-hooks/:trigger/test`           |                                                 | One signed call: `{ ok, failure, statusCode, durationMs }` |
| `GET`    | `/admin/login-hooks/:trigger/invocations`    | `limit` (1 to 100), `outcome`                   | Recent calls, newest first |

A `PUT` replaces every setting and fills the defaults for any you leave out (2000 ms, `closed`,
enabled), so send all four. The CLI's `hooks set` reads the current hook first and changes only
what you name. A disabled or deleted hook is skipped: sign-ins complete as if it did not exist.

The test call sends a placeholder user (`00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000000`, no email, no
roles), no organization and no request details, and is not recorded as an invocation. It passes
when your service answers a body that parses.

Rotation works as it does for webhooks: the old secret keeps signing beside the new one for 24
hours, two `v1` signatures in one header, and rotating again during the overlap ends it at once.

## Example Hook Service

A complete hook service in Node.js with no dependencies. It verifies every call, denies suspended
accounts on `post_login`, and adds a plan and tenant on `pre_token`. Run it with the hook's secret
(both, comma-separated, while it rotates):

```bash
SEAMLESS_HOOK_SECRETS=whsec_... PORT=8787 node hook-service.mjs
```

```js
// hook-service.mjs
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto'
import { createServer } from 'node:http'

const SECRETS = process.env.SEAMLESS_HOOK_SECRETS.split(',')
const TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300

function verified(headers, body) {
  const id = headers['webhook-id']
  const timestamp = headers['webhook-timestamp']
  const signatures = headers['webhook-signature']
  if (!id || !/^\d+$/.test(timestamp ?? '') || !signatures) return false
  if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(timestamp)) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS) return false

  const signed = Buffer.concat([Buffer.from(`${id}.${timestamp}.`), body])
  const expected = SECRETS.map((secret) =>
    createHmac('sha256', Buffer.from(secret.slice('whsec_'.length), 'base64')).update(signed).digest(),
  )
  let valid = false
  for (const entry of signatures.split(' ')) {
    const [version, value] = entry.split(',')
    if (version !== 'v1' || !value) continue
    const received = Buffer.from(value, 'base64')
    for (const digest of expected) {
      if (received.length === digest.length && timingSafeEqual(received, digest)) valid = true
    }
  }
  return valid
}

// Your own rules. These two stand in for a lookup in your database.
const suspended = new Set(['33333333-3333-4333-8333-333333333333'])
const plans = { '11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111': 'enterprise' }

function decide(call) {
  if (call.trigger === 'post_login') {
    if (suspended.has(call.user.id)) {
      return {
        decision: 'deny',
        reason: `account ${call.user.id} is suspended in billing`,
        userMessage: 'Your account is suspended. Contact your administrator.',
      }
    }
    return { decision: 'allow' }
  }
  return {
    decision: 'allow',
    claims: {
      plan: plans[call.user.id] ?? 'free',
      ...(call.organization ? { tenant: call.organization.id } : {}),
    },
  }
}

createServer((req, res) => {
  const chunks = []
  req.on('data', (chunk) => chunks.push(chunk))
  req.on('end', () => {
    const body = Buffer.concat(chunks)
    if (req.method !== 'POST' || !verified(req.headers, body)) {
      res.writeHead(401).end()
      return
    }
    res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': 'application/json' })
    res.end(JSON.stringify(decide(JSON.parse(body.toString('utf8')))))
  })
}).listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 8787))
```

This service was run against calls signed by the auth API's own signer and bodies built with
`LoginHookCallSchema`: an allow, a deny, and a `pre_token` call signed by two secrets parsed with
`PostLoginHookResultSchema` and `PreTokenHookResultSchema`, and the claims passed the API's claim
screen unchanged. A call signed with another secret, or with a timestamp 400 seconds old, got
`401`. A `401` is a failure to the auth API, so a `closed` hook refuses a sign-in it cannot verify.

Do not use `verifyWebhook` from `@seamless-auth/core/webhook` for hook calls: it checks the body
against the webhook event catalog and refuses a hook call as `invalid_payload`. Use a verifier like
the one above, or any of the hand-written ones in the
[webhooks guide](/build/webhooks#step-3-verify-every-request) with the same secret rules.

## Static Custom Claims

A claim set is a JSON object attached to a source:

| Source kind          | Source name           | Reaches |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | ------- |
| `instance_role`      | A role in `available_roles` | First-party tokens and provider tokens of everyone holding the role |
| `organization_role`  | A role in the organization role catalogue | Tokens of members holding it, only while that organization is active |
| `oidc_client`        | An OpenID Provider client id | That client's provider tokens only |

The source must exist when the set is written. Retiring the role or deleting the client deletes its
set, so adding the name back later restores nothing.

### Precedence

When two sources set the same name, the later one wins:

1. Instance role sets, in role name order
2. Organization role sets for the active organization, in role name order
3. The OpenID Provider client's set (provider tokens only)
4. The `pre_token` hook's claims

Role name order means a user holding `billing` and `support` gets `support`'s value for a name
both set, whatever order the roles were granted in.

### Set Them

**Console:** the **Custom claims** page (`/custom-claims` in `seamless-auth-admin-dashboard`)
edits each source's set as JSON, shows the reserved names and the budget the API reports, and
refuses a reserved name, nesting past depth 3 or an oversized set before step-up. It is in the
console from v0.14.0.

**CLI:** `seamless-cli` 0.30.0 and later. `claims set` replaces the whole set and asks
before removing a claim:

```bash
seamless claims set instance_role user '{"plan":"free"}'
seamless claims set organization_role billing '{"can_invoice":true,"limits":{"seats":25}}'
seamless claims set oidc_client grafana --file grafana-claims.json
seamless claims list
seamless claims delete organization_role billing
```

**Admin API:** reads need `admin:read`; writes need `admin:write` and a fresh step-up.

| Method   | Route                                          | Body                | Purpose |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------- | ------- |
| `GET`    | `/admin/custom-claims`                         |                     | Every set, plus `reservedNames`, `reservedPrefixes` and `budgetBytes` |
| `GET`    | `/admin/custom-claims/:sourceKind/:sourceName` |                     | One set. `404` when none |
| `PUT`    | `/admin/custom-claims/:sourceKind/:sourceName` | `{ "claims": {...} }` | Replace the whole set. `404` when the source does not exist |
| `DELETE` | `/admin/custom-claims/:sourceKind/:sourceName` |                     | Delete the set |

```bash
curl -X PUT "$AUTH_SERVER_URL/admin/custom-claims/organization_role/billing" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_ACCESS_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"claims":{"can_invoice":true,"limits":{"seats":25}}}'
```

Writes are audited as `admin_custom_claims_updated` and `admin_custom_claims_deleted`, naming the
claims but not their values.

### Claim Names And Reserved Claims

- **Names** match `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$`: lower case, starting with a letter, up to 64
  characters. No URLs, dots or hyphens.
- **Values** are literal JSON (strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, objects), nested at most 3
  levels. There is no templating.
- **Each set** is at most 1024 bytes serialized as UTF-8 JSON, refused when written over it. A hook's
  claims are held to the same limit.

Reserved names are refused when written and stripped (and audited) when a hook returns them. The
list is `RESERVED_CLAIM_NAMES` and `RESERVED_CLAIM_PREFIXES` in `@seamless-auth/types` 0.39.0
(`customClaim/reserved`), and `GET /admin/custom-claims` returns it:

| Group | Names |
| ----- | ----- |
| JWT registered claims | `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`, `iat`, `jti` |
| Protocol and session  | `azp`, `nonce`, `at_hash`, `c_hash`, `s_hash`, `auth_time`, `acr`, `amr`, `sid`, `scope`, `client_id`, `cnf`, `typ`, `act`, `may_act` |
| Seamless Auth's own   | `roles`, `permissions`, `permissions_omitted`, `org_id`, `org_roles`, `org_permissions`, `recovery` |
| OpenID standard identity claims | `name`, `given_name`, `family_name`, `middle_name`, `nickname`, `preferred_username`, `profile`, `picture`, `website`, `email`, `email_verified`, `gender`, `birthdate`, `zoneinfo`, `locale`, `phone_number`, `phone_number_verified`, `address`, `updated_at` |
| Prefixes              | Any name starting `seamless_` or `org_` |

The identity claims are reserved so that no source can assert an email address or name the user
never proved.

## What Reaches The Token

Custom claims sit at the top level of the access token beside the claims Seamless Auth sets, which
always win:

```json
{
  "plan": "enterprise",
  "tenant": "44444444-4444-4444-8444-444444444444",
  "can_invoice": true,
  "sub": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
  "sid": "session uuid",
  "typ": "access",
  "roles": ["user"],
  "permissions": ["reports:read"],
  "org_id": "44444444-4444-4444-8444-444444444444",
  "org_roles": ["admin", "billing"],
  "org_permissions": ["projects:write"]
}
```

### One Shared 1 KiB Budget

A server adapter keeps the whole access token in a signed cookie under the browser's 4 KiB limit,
so the permission claims (`permissions`, `org_roles`, `org_permissions`) and the merged custom
claims share **one 1024-byte budget**, serialized together. Each token is built by these rules, in
order:

1. If the permission claims and the custom claims fit together, the token carries both.
2. Otherwise **permissions give way first**: the three permission claims are replaced with
   `"permissions_omitted": true`, and the custom claims stay, if they fit beside that marker.
   Permission guards then read `GET /users/me/permissions` live (see
   [How To Use Roles And Permissions](/build/roles-and-permissions#when-the-set-does-not-fit)).
3. Only if the custom claims do not fit even beside the marker are **all** of them dropped. The
   token carries just the marker, and the mint writes the audit event `custom_claims_omitted` with
   the size.
4. Nothing is ever trimmed partially. A recovery token carries neither.

Custom claims have no live fallback, so keep sets small. A hook whose claims alone are over 1 KiB
has failed, and follows its failure mode.

### Provider Tokens

OpenID Provider tokens carry the same values under the same names, released by scope:

| Scope           | Claims |
| --------------- | ------ |
| `permissions`   | `roles`, `permissions`, `org_id`, `org_roles`, `org_permissions`, or `permissions_omitted` |
| `custom_claims` | Every custom claim resolved for the user and this client, including the client's own set and the session's `pre_token` claims |
| `seamless`      | `roles`, `org_id`, unchanged |

ID tokens and `/userinfo` carry them for the scopes granted. A user's access token for a resource
carries them when the grant holds the scope. Session exchange and client credentials tokens carry
none. The auth API computes every value and signs only what it computed, so the provider cannot add
or change a claim. The budget is computed over everything the account has, so a client that asks
only for `permissions` can see `permissions_omitted` because of custom claims it did not ask for.

If a role, membership or claim set changes between the provider reading the account and the API
signing the token, the API refuses the sign with `claims_mismatch`. The provider then reads the
account again and signs once more. A second mismatch, or an account that has gone, fails the token
request with:

```json
{
  "error": "server_error",
  "error_description": "the account changed while the token was being issued, try again"
}
```

with status `500`. The client can retry the request. No other sign refusal is retried.

Provider claims need `seamless-auth-api` v0.23.0 (seamless-auth-api#585) and the provider release
with seamless-auth-oidc-provider#63. Neither is released.

## Porting Auth0 Actions

Auth0's post-login Actions run JavaScript inside Auth0. Seamless Auth runs no code of yours inside
the auth server: the logic moves into your hook service, or into static claims when it only reads
roles.

| Auth0                                                         | Seamless Auth |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| A post-login Action that runs after authentication ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/explore-triggers/signup-and-login-triggers/login-trigger)) | A `post_login` hook to allow or deny, a `pre_token` hook to add claims |
| `api.access.deny(reason)`, whose reason "may be presented directly in end-user interfaces" ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/explore-triggers/signup-and-login-triggers/login-trigger/post-login-api-object)) | `{"decision":"deny","reason":"...","userMessage":"..."}`. Seamless splits the two: `reason` is audited and never shown, `userMessage` is shown |
| `api.idToken.setCustomClaim` and `api.accessToken.setCustomClaim` ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/explore-triggers/signup-and-login-triggers/login-trigger/post-login-api-object)) | `claims` in a `pre_token` answer, or a static set. One set of claims reaches the first-party access token and, with the `custom_claims` scope, provider ID and access tokens alike |
| Claims derived from `event.authorization.roles`, the user's assigned role names ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/explore-triggers/signup-and-login-triggers/login-trigger/post-login-event-object)) | A static set on each role. No code |
| Namespaced claim names such as `https://example.com/plan`, which Auth0 recommends ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/secure/tokens/json-web-tokens/create-custom-claims)) | Rename to the claim alphabet, such as `plan`. URL names are refused |
| Auth0's restricted claims, such as `roles`, `permissions` and `org_id` ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/secure/tokens/json-web-tokens/create-custom-claims)) | The [reserved list](#claim-names-and-reserved-claims). Seamless also reserves the OpenID identity claims such as `email` and `name` |
| A custom claims payload of up to 100 KB ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/secure/tokens/json-web-tokens/create-custom-claims)) | 1 KiB, shared with the permission claims |
| An Action must finish within 20 seconds ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/limitations)) | 2 seconds by default, 5 at most, one attempt, with `open` or `closed` on failure |
| `event.secrets`                                               | Your hook service's own configuration |
| `event.organization`                                          | `organization` in the call: id and the member's roles |
| `api.multifactor.enable` ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/explore-triggers/signup-and-login-triggers/login-trigger/post-login-api-object)) | No hook equivalent. Use Seamless Auth's own sign-in policy and [step-up](/build/totp-step-up) |
| `api.redirect.sendUserTo` ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/explore-triggers/signup-and-login-triggers/login-trigger/post-login-api-object)) | No equivalent. A hook is a server to server call and cannot redirect the browser |
| `api.user.setAppMetadata` ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/explore-triggers/signup-and-login-triggers/login-trigger/post-login-api-object)) | No equivalent. Write to your own database from the hook |
| The post-user-registration trigger, which is asynchronous and cannot affect signup ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/explore-triggers/signup-and-login-triggers/post-user-registration-trigger)) | The [`user.created` webhook](/build/webhooks#event-catalog) |
| Rules, read-only since November 18, 2024 and removed after January 31, 2028 ([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/rules)) | The same mapping as Actions |

### The Difference On Refresh

**Auth0 runs post-login Actions on refresh. Seamless Auth does not run `pre_token` on refresh.**
Auth0's post-login trigger runs when a user authenticates and also when a refresh token is
exchanged
([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/explore-triggers/signup-and-login-triggers/login-trigger)),
and `oauth2-refresh-token` is one of the values of `event.transaction.protocol`
([Auth0 docs](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions/explore-triggers/signup-and-login-triggers/login-trigger/post-login-event-object)).
So an Auth0 Action can recompute a claim, or deny, at every refresh.

In Seamless Auth the `pre_token` claims are fixed for the session, and a refresh never waits on your
server. When you port an Action:

- Move claims that only depend on roles to static sets. Those are recomputed at every token,
  refresh included.
- Keep claims that need your data in `pre_token`, knowing they change at the next sign-in or
  organization switch.
- If the Action denies at refresh (for example a suspension check that should end sessions), do it
  another way: revoke the user's sessions from your system when the account is suspended
  (`DELETE /admin/sessions/:userId/revoke-all`, or the console), and keep the `post_login` hook to
  stop the next sign-in.
- If the Action skips work on refresh by checking `event.transaction.protocol`, drop the check.

### A Ported Action

An Auth0 Action like this:

```js
exports.onExecutePostLogin = async (event, api) => {
  const account = await lookup(event.user.user_id)
  if (account.suspended) {
    api.access.deny('Your account is suspended. Contact your administrator.')
    return
  }
  api.accessToken.setCustomClaim('https://example.com/plan', account.plan)
}
```

becomes the [example hook service](#example-hook-service): the suspension check in `post_login`
with the message as `userMessage`, and the plan in `pre_token` as the claim `plan`. Your backend
reads `plan` from the access token instead of `https://example.com/plan`.

---

## Check It End To End

1. Run the example service and point both hooks at it with `failureMode: "closed"`.
2. Send a test call to each. Expect `ok: true`.
3. Sign in as a normal user. Decode the access token and expect `plan` (and `tenant` in an
   organization). The invocation log shows two `allowed` calls.
4. Add the user's id to `suspended` and sign in again. Expect `403` with
   `{"error":"login_denied","message":"Your account is suspended. Contact your administrator."}`
   and a `login_hook_denied` audit event carrying the `reason`.
5. Stop the service and sign in again. Expect `503 {"error":"login_hook_unavailable"}`. Switch the
   hook to `open` and expect the sign-in to complete, without `plan`.
6. Set a static set on a role you hold, refresh the session, and expect the claim in the new token
   without signing in again.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                                     | Fix |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
| Expecting `pre_token` to run on refresh, as an Auth0 Action does | It runs at sign-in and organization switch. Use static claims for values that must follow role changes |
| Putting internal detail in `userMessage`                    | `userMessage` is shown. Put detail in `reason`, which is only audited |
| A `closed` hook with no redundancy                          | Its outage is a sign-in outage. Run more than one instance, or pick `open` for non-essential hooks |
| A denial that matters on an `open` hook                     | An outage turns it off. Use `closed` |
| Returning `email` or `sub` from a hook                      | Reserved names are stripped. Use your own name |
| Namespaced names like `https://example.com/plan`            | Names match `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$` |
| Large claim sets                                            | One 1 KiB budget is shared with permissions; past it, permissions go first, then every custom claim |
| `PUT /admin/login-hooks/:trigger` with only the field you changed | A `PUT` resets the others to defaults. Send all four, or use `seamless hooks set` |
| Verifying hook calls with `verifyWebhook`                   | It only accepts webhook events. Use the hook service's verifier |
